newsitem.title: UK: SW Water to stem leakage as profits surge.
newsitem.headline: SW Water to stem leakage as profits surge.

text.p: British utility South West Water Plc, posting a surge in profits, said on Thursday it was on track to reduce pipeline leakage to help fight the worst British drought in some 200 years.
South West's pretax profits rose 22 percent to 132.6 million pounds ($217 million) for the year to March 31, including exceptional costs of 5.2 million pounds.
The profits came in line with analysts' expectations, which ranged from 118.0 million to 140.0 million pounds.
The company's shares gained 3.0 pence to trade at 698 by 0945 GMT.
"They are outstanding results," finance director Ken Hill told Reuters in an interview.
"The core utility, water and sewage business was characterised by improving customer service and profitability," he said, adding that non-core operations also produced strong profits.
Hill predicted continued growth, noting that annual earnings per share rose 18.5 percent to 92.1 pence.
"We're well positioned to continue to grow the business, and I see no reason why that shouldn't continue, though not necessarily at that level," he said.
Hill reiterated the company's near-term goal of posting real dividend growth of 8.0 percent per year.
South West raised its full-year dividend by 20 percent to 36.7p.
Hill said the regional utility planned to cut leakage from its pipelines to 15 percent by the end of 1999 from the current level of about 21 percent.
He added that he was not unduly concerned about the government's plan to set targets for cutting leakage at water companies to help combat the country's drought.
"As far as we know, there is nothing in those proposals which will give us cause for major concern," Hill said.
"We've already taken action to reduce leakage, we're continuing to take action, and it's producing significant savings," he added.
Hill said South West had accelerated its two-year plan to invest over 100 million pounds to improve water distribution and cut leakage.
As a result, the company did not see a need for water restrictions this summer, despite the dry period in parts of southwestern England, particularly Cornwall.
"We don't have a water crisis. We don't have any restrictions whatsoever in the southwest. And providing we don't have a very, very dry summer, we don't plan future restrictions," he said.
Hill said it was too early to comment on the new Labour government's plan to introduce a "windfall" tax on the profits of privatised utilities.

"We need to see what the details of the government's proposals are. Until we've see that it would be foolish to say we definitely will not take legal action. But we're certainly not contemplating it," he said.
Hill also said the company would continue to consider non-core acquisitions.
"We've been very successful in non-regulated activities. We certainly wouldn't rule out further acquisitions," he said. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
